data.aborted#Aborted requests: vLLM’s usage chunk comes last. When the client leaves before it, the gateway stops reading (vLLM is not kept generating for nobody) and charges an estimate: prompt bytes / 4 plus the content deltas already forwarded. The record is flagged, in an estimated_requests column of the spend reports and in PostgreSQL. The estimate undercounts tool-call and reasoning tokens.
data.admin-api#Admin API:
Admin routes take Authorization: Bearer or a user’s llma-... token.
Route Purpose GET /admin/whoami the caller and their roles GET, POST /admin/users; DELETE /admin/users/{name}; .../tokens; .../roles users, their tokens and their roles GET, POST /admin/orgs; DELETE /admin/orgs/{name} organisations (one created here has no share: it only borrows) GET /admin/teams?org=, POST /admin/teams; DELETE /admin/teams/{name} teams GET, POST /admin/teams/{team}/projects; DELETE .../projects/{name} projects GET, PUT /admin/teams/{team}/models the model groups a team may use (empty list = every configured model) GET /admin/keys?team=, POST /admin/keys; DELETE /admin/keys/{id} keys (the llmf-... secret is returned once); a key may carry tags GET, PUT /admin/budgets; DELETE /admin/budgets?kind=&name=&model= budgets: {"kind","name","model","period","max_cost","soft_limit"} with period day, week or month POST /admin/budgets/increase a temporary increase with an expiry GET /admin/spend?from=&to=&group_by=&format= spend report grouped by any of org, team, project, key, model, pool, tag; json, csv or parsable2; filtered to what the caller may see GET /admin/usage.csv?from=&to= the v0.1 export GET /admin/fairshare reservations, in-flight, borrowing, usage, level fairshare and rank per pool and organisation A request is refused with 429, naming the scope, as soon as one budget it falls under is exhausted. soft_limit triggers one alert per budget and period, to a webhook and/or by e-mail through an SMTP relay.
data.architecture#Architecture: clients (OpenAI SDKs, Authorization: Bearer llmf-...) | v llmflow-gateway 1 auth: virtual key -> team (SHA-256, constant-time, cached) 2 body <= max_body_bytes, JSON re-encoded, client priority fields stripped, per-tenant cache_salt set 3 budget (GPU-hours per day / week / month), fail-closed by default 4 per-key RPM / TPM / max in-flight 5 fair share: within reservation -> priority 0/1, borrowing -> 10 and more 6 route: least in-flight healthy upstream, retry before the first byte 7 stream SSE event by event, capture usage 8 cost -> budget counter, fair-share usage, async PostgreSQL record | v headers built from scratch: Authorization (internal key), X-Vllm-Priority vLLM x N (--scheduling-policy priority --api-key ..., reachable only from the gateway) Packages: fairshare (the algorithm, no I/O), openai (request rewrite, SSE usage capture), store (memory and PostgreSQL), gateway (HTTP server), config, and cmd/llmflow-gateway (cobra command line).
data.configuration#Configuration (HCL2):
The configuration is written in HCL2 native syntax; the repository’s examples/gateway.hcl is parsed by its test suite, so it stays valid. This extract was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.3.0 (with the key files present):
master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key" cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key" org "etabA" { share = 0.8125 team "lab-nlp" {} team "lab-vision" {} } org "etabB" { share = 0.1875 team "lab-chem" {} } pool "b300" { capacity = 256 } model "llama-3.3-70b" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct" pool = "b300" class = "interactive" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" cost { input_per_mtok = 0.02 output_per_mtok = 0.20 cached_per_mtok = 0.002 } upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://10.0.0.11:8000" } upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://10.0.0.12:8000" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/gpu02.key" } } Block or attribute Meaning org "" { share, team "" {} ... } an organisation (institution) with the fraction of every pool reserved for it (sum at most 1) and the teams declared under it; team names are global pool "" { capacity } C, the sustainable concurrency of the pool (1 to 1048576) model "" { ... } client model name; upstream_model, pool, class (interactive or batch), key_file, cost { input_per_mtok, output_per_mtok, cached_per_mtok } in GPU-hours per million tokens, and upstream "" { base_url, key_file } blocks store { ... } kind (memory or postgres), dsn_file, fail_closed (default true), queue_size, batch_size fairshare { half_life } usage decay half-life (default "168h") limits { ... }, health { ... } body and header sizes, timeouts, maximum request duration and response size; health-check interval, timeout, cooldown and path tags { header, allowed } the request header clients may tag requests with, and the allowed tags cache_isolation, cache_salt_key_file prefix-cache tenant scope (org default, team, key, none) and the HMAC key file (at least 32 bytes; required unless none) alerts { webhook_url, webhook_token_file, smtp { server, from, to, username, password_file } } where soft-budget alerts go auth_failures_per_minute failed authentications allowed per client network before a 429 (default 60, 0 disables) Design decisions of the format:
Static evaluation. The file is decoded with no evaluation context: no variables, no functions. env.HOME, file("/etc/shadow") or "${x}" are errors, so a configuration cannot read the environment or other files. Quoted strings are templates. A literal ${ must be written $${, and a literal %{ must be written %%{. This applies to every value, URLs, paths and model names included. Labelled blocks for named things: org, team, pool, model, upstream. Duplicate labels are errors. Teams nest inside their organisation. Every diagnostic carries file:line:column; check-config prints them one per line. Secrets only by file (master_key_file, metrics_token_file, store.dsn_file, key_file, cache_salt_key_file, and so on). An upstream URL with credentials is rejected. Durations are strings in Go syntax ("30s", "168h"). Absent and zero differ: retries = 0 disables retries, leaving it out takes the default. The parser is fuzzed (FuzzParse): the configuration is treated as untrusted input. Cost of a request, in GPU-hours: ((prompt - cached) x input + cached x cached_price + completion x output) / 10^6, from the usage vLLM reports.
data.fair-share-with-borrowing#How fair-share:
A pool has a capacity C: the concurrency it sustains without preemption, measured externally. Each organisation owns an integer reservation, shared by all its teams and projects, obtained by apportioning C over the shares with the largest-remainder (Hamilton) method, so reservations never sum to more than C (C = 256 gives A 208 and B 48).
For every request:
Situation Priority sent to vLLM the organisation has fewer within-share requests in flight than its reservation 0 interactive, 1 batch otherwise (borrowing) 10 + 10 x rank + class, rank at most 9 Among borrowers, rank is the dense rank of the organisation’s level fairshare LF = S / U (Slurm Fair Tree): the most under-served has rank 0, so the most over-served borrower gets the largest number, is admitted last and is preempted first. Usage is the cost actually consumed, charged when a request finishes and decayed with a half-life (the exact exponential, of which Slurm’s 1 - 0.693/hl is the first-order expansion).
vLLM’s v1 scheduler keeps waiting requests in a min-heap on (priority, arrival_time); when a running request runs out of KV blocks, the running request with the largest (priority, arrival_time) is preempted; a waiting request never preempts a running one. A within-share request is therefore admitted before any borrower and is never the victim while a borrower runs. The guide explains vLLM’s priority semantics from its source.
Two choices were forced by the simulator: the reservation test counts within-share requests in flight (not all requests), and usage is charged at release (not from time in flight, since a request waiting in vLLM’s queue consumes nothing).
Scenario (C = 16, 64 clients per team) Result A alone, B alone KV utilisation 0.98 and 0.97; 40.5 and 39.0 running, for reservations of 13 and 3 both saturating, B arriving after A filled the pool running fraction A 0.789, B 0.211 (shares 0.8125 and 0.1875) preemptions 24,614, every one a borrower control: every request at priority 0 B gets 0.498, its fraction of clients, not its share
data.gateway#gateway: An OpenAI-compatible gateway in pure Go (CGO_ENABLED=0) that sits in front of vLLM on a GPU cluster shared by several institutions. It replaces LiteLLM for that role and adds fair-share scheduling with reservation and borrowing, mapped onto vLLM’s own priority scheduler. Repository →
data.hierarchy#Hierarchy and roles:
The tree mirrors a Slurm account tree: organisation (institution) → team (lab) → project → key. Budgets can be set on every scope (organisation, team, project, key, tag), and for one model group. Administration is delegated by role:
Role Scope May proxy_admin everything everything the master key may proxy_viewer everything read every listing, report and fair-share state org_admin one organisation manage its teams, projects, keys, budgets and users below it team_admin one team manage its projects and keys, grant member and viewer on the team member one team create keys (owned by the member), list and revoke their own keys viewer one organisation or team read its teams, projects, keys (no secrets), budgets and spend Users authenticate with admin tokens (llma-..., 256 random bits, stored as SHA-256, shown once). Nobody can grant a role above their own scope. Teams can restrict which model groups they may use.
data.limitations#Limitations:
Open defects of v0.3.0, as the repository lists them:
State is per process. In-flight counts, rate limits and the key cache live in memory: run one gateway replica per pool. Several replicas would each grant the full reservation. Budgets lag. The cost is known when a request ends, so a burst of long requests can overspend by what is in flight. Several gateways see each other’s spend only at their next refresh. Priority is fixed at admission. A borrowing request already queued in vLLM keeps its priority when its organisation drops back under its reservation, and teams inside an organisation share its reservation without sub-shares of their own. vLLM has no API to re-prioritise a queued request. Aborted requests are charged with an estimate (see above). Prefix-cache isolation is per scope, not absolute (see above). Accounting can drop records when its queue is full or a batch write fails twice (both are counted in metrics); budgets count the cost until the next refresh only. No TLS in the gateway: put it behind a TLS proxy. The admin API shares the client listener. /v1/responses is not proxied. C is static configuration; the gateway does not measure or adapt it. Admin principals are read from the store on every admin request, with no cache: role changes apply at once, but the admin API fails with the store. Soft-budget alerts are sent once and not retried: a webhook or SMTP failure is logged, and the period is already marked as alerted.
data.overhead#Overhead:
Preliminary, measured by the maintainers on a loaded machine (1-minute load 6 to 7.5). gateway/bench_test.go interleaves, on the same client and keep-alive connections, one request straight to an upstream that answers instantly and one through the gateway (memory store; auth, budgets, limits, fair share, accounting and metrics all on the path). Apple M4 Max, one core, 5 runs of 20,000 interleaved pairs; ranges are min to max over the runs.
Added by the gateway v0.1.0 (load 7.8-8.1) v0.2.0 (load 6.3-7.5) p50 54.9-55.3 us 53.2-54.5 us p99 131.2-134.2 us 128.4-143.9 us So about +54 us at p50 and +130 to 144 us at p99 over a direct call. LiteLLM reports its own overhead in a response header, which read 3.2 to 4.9 ms on an instant upstream. That is not a comparison: LiteLLM’s figure is self-reported per request, the gateway’s is an end-to-end difference against a direct call, and the machine was loaded. An independent, interleaved A/B of both gateways on an idle machine is pending; until it is done, no ratio between the two should be taken as established.
data.prefix-cache-isolation#Prefix-cache isol:
Why. vLLM reuses cached KV blocks across requests that share a prompt prefix. That reuse is a timing side channel: a caller can test whether a guessed prefix is already cached by measuring the time to first token, and so learn what another tenant sent. vLLM’s security guide documents it, and it is tracked as CVE-2025-46570. On a cluster shared by several institutions this is a leak between institutions.
What the gateway does. It removes any cache_salt the client sends and always sets its own: base64url(HMAC-SHA256(key, scope)), 43 characters (256 bits). The key is read from cache_salt_key_file, and the scope is set by cache_isolation:
cache_isolation One prefix cache per org (default) organisation (institution) team team key virtual key none nothing: a single tenant vLLM mixes the salt into the hash of the first KV block and every later block chains from it, so different scopes never share cached blocks. The salt is stable per scope (a random salt per request would disable prefix caching). Multimodal uuid values in the message content parts are rewritten per tenant, not stripped: a client can keep referring to media it sent earlier, while the same uuid sent by two tenants names two different cache entries.
Operating it. cache_salt_key_file must hold at least 32 random bytes and be readable by its owner only (mode 0600); it is mandatory unless cache_isolation = "none". Rotating the key means a cold prefix cache for everyone.
Residual risk. Within one scope the cache is shared. With the default org, users of the same institution can still probe each other by timing; team or key narrow that, at the cost of less cache reuse. And vLLM itself states that cache_salt is not an isolation boundary: tenants that need hard isolation need a vLLM instance of their own.
data.roadmap#Roadmap: Issue #7 tracks shipping every LiteLLM Enterprise feature in the open-source gateway. M1 (governance and multi-tenancy) is done, in v0.2.0. Next come M2 (identity and access: OpenID Connect, JWT, SCIM, key rotation, IP allowlists, secret managers), M3 (audit and logging) and M4 (guardrails). The version numbers written in the issue shift by one: v0.3.0 was taken by the security patch above, so M2 is not v0.3.0 any more.
data.routes#Routes: Client routes: POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /v1/completions, POST /v1/embeddings, GET /v1/models. Also GET /healthz, which returns 503 when the budget state is stale and fail-closed is on, and GET /metrics (Prometheus text format, optional bearer token). /v1/responses is not proxied.
data.security#Security: Clients cannot choose their priority. The body is parsed and re-encoded (duplicate keys and escaped spellings cannot survive); priority, extra_body, request_id, kv_transfer_params, ec_transfer_params and vllm_xargs are removed. Upstream headers are built from scratch, so a client’s X-Vllm-Priority, x-pass-*, Authorization and X-Forwarded-* never reach vLLM. This closes a hole measured on LiteLLM. The rewrite and the SSE copier are fuzzed (FuzzRewrite, FuzzCopySSE). vLLM must only be reachable from the gateway. Its --api-key covers only /v1, /v2 and /inference; /invocations exposes inference without authentication. Firewall the vLLM ports (guide). Keys. Virtual keys and admin tokens are 256-bit random secrets, stored as SHA-256, compared in constant time and shown once. Secrets come from files only and never appear in logs, errors or listings. No SSRF. Upstreams come from the configuration only; client input selects a model group, never a URL. Upstream redirects are not followed. Brute force. Failed authentications are limited per client network (IPv4 address or IPv6 /64, from the connection, not from proxy headers) by auth_failures_per_minute; valid and missed keys live in two separate bounded caches, so a spray of random keys cannot evict valid ones. Limits on body, headers, timeouts, request duration and upstream response size; a bounded accounting queue. Budgets fail closed: when PostgreSQL cannot be read for 3 refresh periods, every request gets 503 (fail_closed = false to fail open). CI: race tests on amd64 and arm64, PostgreSQL integration tests, fuzz smoke, govulncheck, CGO_ENABLED=0 cross-builds.

data.upgrading#Upgrading: From v0.1 to v0.2. Shares are now per organisation: team "x" { share } becomes org "x" { share = ... team "lab" {} }. In the admin API, PUT /admin/budgets takes {"kind","name","model","period","max_cost","soft_limit"} and DELETE takes ?kind=&name=&model=. The fair-share metrics carry the label org. From v0.2 to v0.3. cache_salt_key_file is mandatory unless cache_isolation = "none". The first start with a new key, and every key rotation, leaves every tenant with a cold prefix cache.

data.fair-share#Fair-share on a co-owned GPU:
How to share four HGX B300 servers (32 GPUs) between two institutions, A and B, with Slurm for batch computing, vLLM for inference, a gateway for keys and quotas, and VS Code to reach it all. The sharing must respect each institution’s share and leave no GPU idle.
This is an English adaptation of a design and operations document, version 1.1 of 23 October 2026. Every parameter cited refers to the vendors’ documentation consulted on that date (see the bibliography). The measurements are real and dated: they were made on LiteLLM 1.106.2 on 23 October 2026.
The guide has three layers, one page each:
Slurm guarantees each institution its share (QOS caps, preemption of borrowing jobs) and divides the rest by fair-share (the Fair Tree algorithm): Slurm. vLLM serves the language models in long Slurm jobs, and a gateway in front of it authenticates users, applies per-institution quotas and counts consumption in tokens: Inference. One accounting, in GPU-hours, ties the two: Accounting. Then VS Code access, the security audit, acceptance tests and governance, and the bibliography.
data.hardware#The hardware:
Each server is an HGX B300 with 8 Blackwell Ultra SXM GPUs linked by NVLink 5. Figures are NVIDIA’s (the HGX datasheet, the Blackwell Ultra technical blog and the DGX B300 user guide).
per GPU per server (8 GPUs) HBM3e memory 288 GB 2.3 TB (8 x 288); 2.1 TB on the HGX datasheet HBM bandwidth 8 TB/s – NVLink 5, GPU to GPU (bidirectional) 1.8 TB/s 14.4 TB/s in total NVFP4, dense / sparse 15 / 20 PFLOPS 108 / 144 PFLOPS FP8, dense / sparse 5 / 10 PFLOPS 36 / 72 PFLOPS FP64 – 10 TFLOPS INT8 (sparse) – 3 POPS (72 on HGX B200) MIG partitions up to 7 instances (for example 7 x 34 GB) – Power TGP up to 1,400 W DGX B300: 14.5 kW, 15 kW max Per-GPU and per-server figures are not always in a ratio of 8: 108/8 = 13.5 PFLOPS rather than 15, and 2.1 TB rather than 8 x 288 GB. NVIDIA states that memory and SM count vary by part number. Use the values of your vendor’s datasheet. As an example, the DGX B300 has 2 Xeon Platinum 6776P and 2 TB of RAM (up to 4).
The B300 is an AI machine, not a double-precision scientific one. 10 TFLOPS of FP64 for 8 GPUs, and an INT8 rate divided by 24 relative to the B200. A classic FP64 code (CFD, quantum chemistry, finite elements) wastes its institution’s share here. The agreement between the institutions should say so; such codes belong on other facilities. The cluster has 32 GPUs. A practical consequence: a model served with tensor parallelism 8 (--tensor-parallel-size 8) occupies a whole server, because NVLink does not connect two servers.
data.hybrid#The hybrid model in one sentence:
By default each institution submits to its own owner QOS, capped at its share; those jobs are never preempted. Beyond its share it submits to the borrow QOS, uncapped but preemptible by the owner QOS. Among waiting jobs, the order depends on fair-share, which penalises the institution that consumed more than its share over the last two weeks.
VS Code ──HTTPS──> gateway (keys, teams, quotas, accounting) ──internal──> vLLM (Continue, (Slurm jobs, Remote-SSH) QOS service) └──SSH──> login node (sbatch, srun) ──> slurmctld + slurmdbd ──> gpu01 ... gpu04 (Fair Tree, QOS, preemption) 4 x 8 B300
data.objectives#Objectives: Guarantee: each institution gets its share (26 or 6 GPUs) within a bounded, known delay, even when the cluster is full. No loss: a GPU its owner does not use is lent to the other institution. Fairness over time: over a sliding window, each one’s consumption tends to its share. Whoever borrowed a lot goes behind the other. One accounting: batch and inference are both read in GPU-hours, for re-invoicing and governance. Security: GPU isolation between jobs, and no inference service reachable without authentication.
data.ownership#Ownership:
Institution A bought 3 whole servers and the remaining quarter of the 4th; institution B bought the other three quarters of the 4th. If a later purchase changes the split, update this table and the values derived from it (Fairshare, GrpTRES).
Institution Servers GPUs Share Slurm Fairshare A 3 + 1/4 26 81.25 % 26 B 3/4 6 18.75 % 6 Total 4 32 100 % 32 Slurm shares are expressed in GPUs, which keeps them readable. Slurm normalises against siblings (S = S_self / S_(self+siblings)), so only the ratio 26:6 counts.
data.three-models#Three possible models: Model Advantages Drawbacks Fixed partitions simple; immediate guarantee GPUs lost when the owner is idle; B can never run a TP=8 job (8 GPUs) Pure fair-share no GPU lost; fairness in the long run no guarantee on the delay: B may wait for A’s long jobs to end Hybrid (chosen) bounded guarantee, lending of surplus, fairness preemption: borrowed jobs must be able to resume (checkpoint)

data.accounting#One accounting:
Batch is counted in GPU-equivalent hours (sreport, after TRESBillingWeights). Inference is counted in tokens, per team (the gateway’s spend logs). They are reconciled as follows:
Over the period (a month), read the GPU-hours of the svc_llm account: H_svc. Read each team’s spend in the gateway: D_A, D_B. Charge H_svc x D_A / (D_A + D_B) to A, and the remainder to B. Compare each institution’s total consumption (batch plus charged inference) with its share (81.25 % / 18.75 %).
data.calibration#Calibrating the internal cos:
Goal: 1 unit of gateway spend = 1 GPU-hour. A saturated 8-GPU instance then “spends” 8 units per hour, and max_budget becomes a quota of inference GPU-hours, directly comparable with batch.
1. Measure the capacity. Once per model and per configuration (TP, KV-cache dtype), with vllm bench serve [24]. Use a mix of lengths representative of the real usage (for example 2,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens for a code assistant). Raise --max-concurrency up to the limit of the service target, for instance a p99 time to first token under 2 s:
vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \ --host gpu01.internal --port 8000 --model \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 300 \ --num-prompts 2000 --max-concurrency 64 --save-result At the chosen concurrency C (which also serves the fair-share relay), read the output throughput T_out and the total throughput T_tot in tokens/s, printed by the tool [24]. The input throughput is T_in = T_tot - T_out.
2. Split the cost of an instance-hour. Prefill (input) costs much less per token than generation. Fix a ratio r = c_out / c_in, typically r = 4, and solve:
3600 (c_in T_in + c_out T_out) = 8 => c_in = 8 / (3600 (T_in + r T_out)), c_out = r c_in A fictitious example, to illustrate the computation (the real figures come out of step 1): T_in = 40,000, T_out = 6,000 tokens/s, r = 4. Then c_in = 8 / (3600 x 64,000) = 3.5e-8 and c_out = 1.4e-7 unit per token.
3. Tokens served from the prefix cache. LiteLLM warns that a model with custom pricing bills these tokens at 0 as long as cache_read_input_token_cost is not set (a warning observed at LiteLLM 1.106.2 start-up). Set it to about c_in / 10: these tokens are not recomputed, but they occupy KV memory.
Why not a cost per second? LiteLLM accepts cost_per_second [22]. But vLLM processes dozens of requests simultaneously on one instance: billing each by its duration would make it pay for the whole instance, and the sum would far exceed the real 8 GPU-hours. The per-token cost is the right model.
Recalibrate at each change of model, vLLM version or KV-cache dtype, and check once a month. The GPU-hours of the svc_llm account read from sreport should stay close to the month’s total gateway spend divided by the average occupancy.
data.compensation#Compensation: If, over a quarter, an institution consumed markedly more than its share through inference, the committee may correct the Slurm Fairshare values of the next quarter. Batch fair-share already rebalances by itself within the half-life window: compensation is only an exceptional adjustment.

data.acceptance#Acceptance tests: prove the g:
Every guarantee is proven by a test that could fail:
B’s guarantee. A fills the 32 GPUs (13 in instA, 19 in borrow). B submits 3 GPUs in instB. Measure the start delay: it must stay under 36 minutes, and under 6 minutes if the borrowed jobs are older than 30 minutes. Negative control. The same scenario with the borrow QOS without Preempt: B must wait. If B starts anyway, test 1 was not measuring preemption. Cap. B submits 8 GPUs in instB: immediate rejection (DenyOnLimit). Fair-share. After a week in which B borrows heavily, sshare -l must show LF_B < 1, and A’s borrow jobs must go ahead of B’s (sprio). Billing. A job of 1 GPU and 64 cores must be billed 4: the billing= field of AllocTRES in sacct. Inference. Saturate the model with a key of A; check that a key of B still gets about 18.75 % of the throughput (with the Enterprise reservation, or the relay) or its static limit. vLLM priority. During saturation, a request of the large-model group (priority 0) must have a time to first token markedly lower than a request of large-model-batch (priority 10). Inviolable priority. Send to large-model-batch a request with extra_body: {"priority": 0} and a header X-Vllm-Priority: 0. It must stay processed at priority 10. Control: the same request sent directly to vLLM goes ahead. B’s window. One hour before instB_weekly opens, submit in borrow a 3 h job and a 30 min job. Only the second must start on the reserved server. At opening, an 8-GPU job of B must start immediately. Performance. Compare throughput (tokens/s) and latency (time to first token, p50/p99) of vLLM behind the gateway with those of vLLM direct, at equal load. The gateway’s overhead must stay negligible next to generation; if it does not, increase the number of gateway workers before touching vLLM.
data.governance#Governance: Agreement between institutions: shares (26/6), guaranteed delay (36 min), size of the inference pool, half-life (14 days), the quarterly compensation rule, and the possible reservation of a whole server for B. Quarterly technical committee: real consumption against share, median wait times per institution and per QOS, preemption rate, inference saturation. Change of shares (the purchase of a 5th server, say): change the Fairshare and GrpTRES values. No redeployment is needed.

data.alternatives#Alternatives without a lice:
Synthesis of each product’s official documentation, consulted on 23 October 2026. Y = native; P = partial; – = absent; $ = paid offer. Columns: keys and teams, rate limits, budgets, spreading between instances, reservation with lending.
Gateway Keys Limits Budgets Spread Lending Remarks LiteLLM (MIT, Python) Y Y Y Y $ lending = Enterprise beta [14] Bifrost (Apache-2.0, Go) [26] ? Y Y P – teams described in the free docs, but “governance across teams and customers” is listed as Enterprise: to test Apache APISIX (Apache-2.0) [27] Y Y P Y – standalone YAML mode + Redis, no Kubernetes Envoy AI Gateway [28] – Y P P – token-based limits; Kubernetes required Gateway API Inference Ext. / llm-d [29] – – – Y P routing on KV cache; Kubernetes required; weighted fairness announced as “planned” vLLM production-stack [30] – – – Y – router only Portkey (MIT) [31] $ ? ? Y – key management is paid Kong AI Gateway [32] $ $ – $ – advanced plugins are Enterprise No free gateway natively provides lending with a guarantee. The only project that comes close (llm-d, weighted fairness) requires Kubernetes and still calls it “planned”. For a cluster without Kubernetes: free LiteLLM plus a relay covers the five needs without a licence and keeps the keys, budgets and accounts described here. Bifrost, written in Go, is an alternative to evaluate if its teams turn out to be free; the relay would plug into it the same way.
data.elastic-pool#Elastic pool: At night and at weekends interactive inference drops. An scontrol update or a scrontab can stop one instance in two: 8 GPUs go back to the borrow QOS, without changing A’s and B’s guarantees. On the gateway side the second instance leaves the routing; its requests go to the first, which stays available.
data.fair-share-inference#Fair-share for infe:
LiteLLM’s dynamic_rate_limiter_v3 shares a model’s TPM/RPM capacity between teams. Below a saturation threshold anyone may borrow the free capacity. Above it, each priority is brought back to its reserved share [14]. It is a direct transposition of the Slurm model: lending of surplus, guarantee at saturation.
litellm_settings: callbacks: ["dynamic_rate_limiter_v3"] priority_reservation: instA: 0.8125 instB: 0.1875 saturation_threshold: 0.8 A key’s priority comes from its team’s metadata.priority, which wins over the key’s. Keys with no priority fall into a common pool (default_priority, 0.25 by default) [14]. The model’s capacity (rpm/tpm of the deployments) is measured in acceptance on your B300s, at the target latency.
(1) Priority reservation is marked beta and requires a LiteLLM Enterprise licence (30-day free trial) [14]. (2) Borrowed capacity is not taken back when strict mode engages, and TPM is checked at admission: a burst can exceed the limit. (3) With several LiteLLM instances, strict mode may engage late on a node that has not seen the traffic (60 s cache by default) [14].
data.fairq#Split with lending, without a lice:
Free-edition LiteLLM provides keys, teams, budgets and static limits (tpm_limit, rpm_limit, max_parallel_requests) [11]. What is missing is the lending. Static limits at 81.25 / 18.75 leave an absent institution’s share unused.
The proposal is to reproduce the Slurm scheme (guaranteed share plus preemptible borrowing) at request level: a small relay between the gateway and vLLM counts the requests in flight per institution. Let C be the sustainable concurrency of an instance, measured (see accounting).
If the institution has fewer than p x C requests in flight (p = 0.8125 or 0.1875), the request is within its share: X-Vllm-Priority is 0 (interactive) or 1 (batch). Otherwise it is borrowing: priority 10 (interactive) or 11 (batch). The relay overwrites any priority and any X-Vllm-Priority coming from the client. vLLM then does exactly what is expected (see priority): within-share requests are admitted before borrowing ones; when KV memory runs short, borrowers are preempted first. Without competition an institution takes everything; under saturation each gets its share back.
This is the policy the gateway (v0.3.0) implements in its fairshare package, with the two refinements the simulator forced (the reservation test counts within-share requests, and usage is charged at release). It replaces LiteLLM and the relay here: it holds the keys, organisations, teams and budgets itself, and the shares belong to the organisations (the institutions). For this cluster, its configuration (HCL2, not YAML) would be as follows, with the 256-request capacity of the gateway’s example. This block was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.3.0, with the key files present:
master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key" cache_isolation = "org" cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key" org "instA" { share = 0.8125 team "a-physics" {} team "a-biology" {} } org "instB" { share = 0.1875 team "b-lab" {} } pool "b300" { capacity = 256 } model "large-model" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct" pool = "b300" class = "interactive" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" cost { input_per_mtok = 0.02 output_per_mtok = 0.20 cached_per_mtok = 0.002 } upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://gpu01.internal:8000" } upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://gpu02.internal:8000" } } # the same upstreams again, with class = "batch" model "large-model-batch" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct" pool = "b300" class = "batch" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" cost { input_per_mtok = 0.02 output_per_mtok = 0.20 cached_per_mtok = 0.002 } upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://gpu01.internal:8000" } upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://gpu02.internal:8000" } } The cost values are in GPU-hours per million tokens; calibrate them as in the accounting page. Note the gateway’s limitations, in particular one replica per pool.
To validate: how the relay knows the institution. Two routes. (a) One deployment per institution (api_base: http://relay:9000/instA/v1), reachable only by the team’s keys: safe, but one must check how LiteLLM exposes a single model name to two teams. (b) The X-Litellm-User_api_key_* headers that LiteLLM adds with add_user_information_to_llm_headers: we observed them (user id, key fingerprint). The presence of the team id could not be verified, because our test ran without a database, hence without teams.
data.inference#Inference: Shared inference is vLLM running inside Slurm, behind a gateway that is the only HTTPS entry point. In the original design the gateway is LiteLLM; the measurements below are of LiteLLM 1.106.2. The Go gateway of this organisation implements the fair-share policy that LiteLLM’s free edition lacks.
data.prefix-cache-isolation#Prefix-cache isol: With --enable-prefix-caching, vLLM reuses cached KV blocks across requests that share a prompt prefix. That reuse is a timing side channel between tenants: a caller can tell from the time to first token whether a guessed prefix was cached, hence whether another institution sent it (vLLM’s security guide; CVE-2025-46570). On a cluster shared by A and B this must be closed. The vLLM mechanism is the cache_salt request field, mixed into the hash of the first KV block. The Go gateway (v0.3.0) always sets a stable per-tenant salt (an HMAC of the tenant under a secret key file of at least 32 random bytes) and drops the client’s own; cache_isolation chooses the tenant (org by default, team, key, or none). Two limits to keep in mind: users inside one scope can still probe each other (team or key narrow it, at the cost of cache reuse), and cache_salt is not a hard isolation boundary, which only a vLLM instance per tenant is. Rotating the key empties everyone’s cache.
data.priority#Per-request priority:
A request may carry an integer priority: the lower it is, the sooner the request runs (default 0). The X-Vllm-Priority header takes precedence over the JSON body. Any non-zero value is an error if the server was not started with --scheduling-policy priority [10].
What the scheduler does, from its source code [25]:
the waiting queue is a heap sorted by (priority, arrival_time): the smallest priority comes out first, arrival breaks ties; when a running request cannot find KV-cache blocks any more, vLLM preempts the running request with the largest (priority, arrival_time) and puts it back at the head of the queue; a high-priority waiting request does not preempt a running request: it takes the first slot that frees up. Priority therefore orders admission and designates the victims when memory runs short. It does not interrupt generations in progress. Since a generation lasts a few seconds, the effect on latency is quick. We use it to put interactive use (VS Code, chat) ahead of API batch processing, and for the split between institutions (below).
data.routing#Models and routing:
This is LiteLLM’s configuration; the interactive group pins priority 0 and the batch group pins priority 10, on the same instances.
model_list: # Interactive group (VS Code, chat): vLLM priority pinned to 0 - model_name: large-model litellm_params: model: hosted_vllm/ api_base: http://gpu01.internal:8000/v1 api_key: os.environ/VLLM_INTERNAL_KEY extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "0"} model_info: &cost # internal cost, calibrated on the accounting page input_cost_per_token: output_cost_per_token: cache_read_input_token_cost: - model_name: large-model litellm_params: model: hosted_vllm/ api_base: http://gpu02.internal:8000/v1 api_key: os.environ/VLLM_INTERNAL_KEY extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "0"} model_info: *cost # Batch group (API scripts): same instances, priority 10 - model_name: large-model-batch litellm_params: model: hosted_vllm/ api_base: http://gpu01.internal:8000/v1 api_key: os.environ/VLLM_INTERNAL_KEY extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "10"} model_info: *cost # (... same for gpu02 ...) router_settings: routing_strategy: least-busy allowed_fails: 3 cooldown_time: 30 redis_host: os.environ/REDIS_HOST redis_port: os.environ/REDIS_PORT redis_password: os.environ/REDIS_PASSWORD general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL Two deployments sharing a model_name form a group, and the routing strategy spreads requests between them. least-busy picks the deployment with the fewest calls in progress. A failing deployment goes into cooldown alone, not the whole group [13].
Zero costs = budgets ignored. A model whose two costs are 0 is subject to no budget check [11]. The model is hosted locally, but it must still be given an internal cost, calibrated in GPU-hours (see accounting). Otherwise max_budget protects nothing. Costs are declared under model_info [22]. Measured on LiteLLM 1.106.2: without a cost, spend stays at 0; with a cost, it equals exactly 3 c_in + 1 c_out for 3 input tokens and 1 output token.
data.securing-vllm#Securing vLLM: --api-key protects only the /v1, /v2 and /inference paths. Other endpoints of the same server, such as /invocations, are not authenticated. The documentation asks not to rely on --api-key alone and to put vLLM behind a proxy [10]. Hence the rules: vLLM listens on the cluster’s internal interface only; a firewall lets only the gateway reach the vLLM ports; the internal key is read from a file, never passed in clear in the environment or in shell history.
data.teams-keys#Teams, keys and limits:
# One team per institution (indicative values) curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/team/new \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.config/litellm/master)" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"team_alias": "instA", "max_budget": 1300, "budget_duration": "30d", "max_parallel_requests": 200, "metadata": {"priority": "instA"}}' curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/team/new ... \ -d '{"team_alias": "instB", "max_budget": 300, "budget_duration": "30d", "max_parallel_requests": 50, "metadata": {"priority": "instB"}}' # One key per user, attached to their team curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/key/generate ... \ -d '{"team_id": "", "key_alias": "bob-vscode", "rpm_limit": 60, "max_parallel_requests": 8}' A key that carries a team_id is governed by the team’s budget, not by its owner’s personal budget. The limits tpm_limit, rpm_limit and max_parallel_requests can be set on the team, the user or the key. For one per-model limit, the key’s wins over the team’s [11]. The budget resets at each budget_duration [11].
Do not pass the secret on the command line. The examples read the master key from a file readable by its owner only, never from an environment variable or an argument visible in ps.
data.the-gateway#The gateway:
The gateway is the only HTTPS entry point of inference. It carries:
identity: a virtual key per user, attached to a team = an institution; quotas: rate (tokens/min, requests/min, concurrent requests) and a budget per team; the 81.25 / 18.75 split under saturation; accounting: spend in tokens per team, the basis of the re-charging. With LiteLLM, budgets are enforced only with a Postgres database. Without one they are not enforced at all [11]. With several LiteLLM instances Redis is needed too, or each instance counts on its own and limits can be exceeded. Enable fail_closed_budget_enforcement and fail_closed_rate_limit_enforcement: if Redis or the database fails, the gateway answers 503 instead of letting requests through uncounted [11].
data.vllm-in-slurm#vLLM in Slurm:
Each vLLM instance is a long Slurm job in the svc_llm account and the service QOS. It is therefore accounted, cgroup-isolated, and never preempted. For a whole server:
#!/bin/bash #SBATCH -A svc_llm --qos=service #SBATCH --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:b300:8 --exclusive #SBATCH --time=7-00:00:00 --job-name=vllm-large-model vllm serve \ --host --port 8000 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --scheduling-policy priority \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --max-num-seqs 256 \ --api-key "$(cat /etc/vllm/internal-key)" Option Role (from the engine arguments documentation [9]) --tensor-parallel-size number of tensor-parallel groups; 8 = one NVLink server --data-parallel-size replicas; for MoE models experts are spread over TP x DP --enable-expert-parallel expert parallelism instead of tensor parallelism for MoE layers --scheduling-policy fcfs (default) or priority: order by priority, then arrival --max-num-seqs maximum number of sequences per iteration --max-num-batched-tokens maximum number of tokens per iteration --gpu-memory-utilization share of GPU memory given to vLLM (default 0.92) --enable-prefix-caching reuses the KV cache of common prefixes (shared system prompts) --kv-cache-dtype KV cache type (fp8, nvfp4…): more context in memory --enable-lora, --max-loras per-team LoRA adapters on one base model
data.what-litellm-forwards#What LiteLLM forwa:
The documentation does not say what reaches vLLM. We measured it on 23 October 2026. A real LiteLLM 1.106.2 was placed in front of a fake vLLM written in Go that records every request it receives: path, headers, JSON body. Control: a request sent directly to the fake vLLM with priority: 99 and the header X-Vllm-Priority: 99 shows up intact. So the instrument does see what it looks for.
Sent by the client to LiteLLM Received by vLLM "priority": 10 in the body nothing: LiteLLM consumes this field for its own beta scheduler [15] (response header x-litellm-request-prioritization-used, +300 ms latency) "extra_body": {"priority": 3} "priority": 3 in the body deployment extra_body: {priority: 5} + client extra_body at 0 "priority": 0: the client overrides the deployment’s value deployment extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "6"} X-Vllm-Priority: 6 same + client X-Vllm-Priority: 0, client headers forwarded [23] X-Vllm-Priority: "0, 6": values merged, no longer an integer same + client X-Vllm-Priority: 0 and x-pass-X-Vllm-Priority: 1, default settings X-Vllm-Priority: 6: the client’s headers do not pass Conclusion: the only safe configuration.
Pin the priority by header in the deployment (extra_headers), never by extra_body. Leave forward_client_headers_to_llm_api disabled (the default). A client can still slip priority into the body through extra_body. But vLLM gives the header precedence over the body [10], so the pinned header wins. Do not use LiteLLM’s own priority field: it enables a beta scheduler that adds latency. The class of service (interactive or batch) is then chosen by the model name (large-model or large-model-batch). The keys of batch scripts are restricted to the second.

data.billing#Measuring consumption: GPU billi:
By default consumption is measured in CPU x seconds [2]. On a GPU cluster that is wrong: a job taking 1 core and 8 GPUs would cost almost nothing. So TRESBillingWeights is set on the partition [2], with PriorityFlags=MAX_TRES. A job’s billing then becomes the per-node maximum of the weighted TRES (CPU, memory, GRES) [2], not their sum.
The weights are calibrated so that a whole server is worth 8 units, whichever resource saturates it. For a server of C cores and M GiB of allocatable memory:
w_GPU = 1 w_CPU = 8 / C w_Mem = 8 / M With C = 128 and M = 3072 GiB: CPU=0.0625,Mem=0.0026G,GRES/gpu=1.0. A job taking 1 GPU but 64 cores is billed 4 units, because it makes 4 GPUs unusable for others. The unit of account becomes the GPU-equivalent second.
To validate: replace C and M by the values of slurmd -C [5] on your servers (CPUs and RealMemory minus the memory reserved for the system).
data.decay#Decay of consumption: PriorityDecayHalfLife is 7 days by default and applies every PriorityCalcPeriod (5 minutes by default) [2]. We recommend 14 days: training jobs on B300 often last several days, and a too-short half-life would erase a consumption debt before the other institution could catch up. PriorityUsageResetPeriod stays NONE: an abrupt reset creates edge effects at the start of a period.
data.fair-tree#The Fair Tree algorithm:
Fair Tree has been Slurm’s default since 19.05 [2]. At each level of the association tree it computes the Level Fairshare [1]:
LF = S / U S = S_self / S_(self+siblings) U = U_self / U_(self+siblings) LF > 1 means under-served; LF < 1, over-served; LF = infinity with no consumption. Siblings are sorted by decreasing LF, the tree is walked depth first, and each user receives a rank. The user’s fair-share factor is rank / number of users: 1.0 for the first [1].
The decisive property for us: the first level compares A against B before looking at users. If A is over-served, all of B’s users come before all of A’s, whatever individual consumption is. This is exactly the wanted behaviour between two institutions.
A worked example. Over the last 14 days (with decay), A consumed 70 % of the billed GPU-hours and B 30 %:
LF_A = 0.8125 / 0.70 = 1.16 LF_B = 0.1875 / 0.30 = 0.625 A is under-served relative to its share, so it goes first: its users get the highest ranks. B’s borrowing jobs will wait until A’s usage is back to normal. B’s jobs in its owner QOS remain guaranteed (see QOS).
data.gres-cgroup#gres.conf and cgroup.conf:
# gres.conf -- automatic detection through NVML AutoDetect=nvml # cgroup.conf ConstrainCores=yes ConstrainDevices=yes ConstrainRAMSpace=yes With AutoDetect=nvml, Slurm fills in the details of detected GPUs. The Gres= line of slurm.conf stays mandatory, and a node exposing fewer GPUs than announced goes to DRAIN [5].
ConstrainDevices=yes limits a job to the devices of its GRES allocation [7]. Without it a job could open another institution’s GPUs.
MIG (optional). For small inference or TP jobs, the B300s can be cut into MIG instances. Slurm manages them with AutoDetect=nvml on the nodes concerned, each instance typed by its profile [5]. Shards, on the other hand, do not partition processes on the GPU [5]: reserve them for uses inside one institution.
data.monitoring#Monitoring: Command What it shows sshare -l each association’s Level FS [1]: are A and B over- or under-served? sprio -l decomposition of the priority of waiting jobs by factor sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser -T gres/gpu GPU-hours per account over a period scontrol show job the PreemptEligibleTime [3] of a borrowed job
data.multifactor#Multifactor priority: With PriorityType=priority/multifactor, a job’s priority is an integer: a site factor, plus the sum of each factor (age, association, fair-share, size, partition, QOS, TRES) times its weight, minus the nice value. Each factor is between 0 and 1 and weights default to 0, so only the configured factors count [2].
data.preemption#Preemption:
PreemptType=preempt/qos: the rules come from the QOS in the database [3]. PreemptMode=REQUEUE: the preempted job is put back in the queue. This requires JobRequeue=1 or sbatch --requeue [3]. SUSPEND is rejected: a suspended job keeps its memory, hence its 288 GB of HBM per GPU, and the owner QOS would recover nothing [3]. PreemptExemptTime: minimum run time before being preemptible [3]. We choose 30 min, so that a borrowed job makes at least some progress. GraceTime on the borrow QOS: the delay between SIGTERM and SIGKILL [3], used to write a checkpoint. We choose 300 s. Guaranteed delay. An owner job that fits in its QOS starts after at most
PreemptExemptTime + GraceTime + one scheduling cycle = 30 + 5 + 1 = 36 minutes and in practice much sooner, since most borrowed jobs have already passed their first 30 minutes. This figure goes into the agreement between institutions and is measured in the acceptance tests.
data.sacctmgr#Accounts and QOS (sacctmgr): # Institutions: shares expressed in owned GPUs sacctmgr add account instA Description="Institution A" Fairshare=26 sacctmgr add account instB Description="Institution B" Fairshare=6 sacctmgr add account svc_llm Description="Inference service" Fairshare=1 Parent=root # Teams (example) under each institution sacctmgr add account a_physics Parent=instA Fairshare=60 sacctmgr add account a_biology Parent=instA Fairshare=40 sacctmgr add account b_lab Parent=instB Fairshare=parent # QOS sacctmgr add qos borrow sacctmgr modify qos borrow set Priority=0 PreemptMode=REQUEUE GraceTime=300 sacctmgr add qos instA sacctmgr modify qos instA set Priority=100 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=13 \ Preempt=borrow Flags=DenyOnLimit sacctmgr add qos instB sacctmgr modify qos instB set Priority=100 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=3 \ Preempt=borrow Flags=DenyOnLimit sacctmgr add qos service sacctmgr modify qos service set Priority=1000 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 Preempt=borrow # Attachment: owner QOS by default + the right to borrow sacctmgr modify account instA set QOS=instA,borrow DefaultQOS=instA sacctmgr modify account instB set QOS=instB,borrow DefaultQOS=instB sacctmgr modify account svc_llm set QOS=service DefaultQOS=service # Users sacctmgr add user alice Account=a_physics sacctmgr add user bob Account=b_lab Fairshare=parent on an account attaches its children to the parent for the computation [8]: B, which has a single laboratory, adds no useless level. DenyOnLimit rejects at submission a job that alone would exceed the QOS limits [8]. An 8-GPU job submitted in instB is refused immediately instead of waiting forever; the user is invited to use borrow. svc_llm receives a symbolic share: its guarantee comes from the service QOS, not from fair-share. Its consumption is re-charged to the institutions (see accounting).
data.slurm#Slurm: Slurm carries the batch workload and the guarantee. Reference numbers are [n] entries of the bibliography.
data.slurm-conf#slurm.conf (excerpts):
ClusterName=b300 SelectType=select/cons_tres SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory GresTypes=gpu NodeName=gpu[01-04] Gres=gpu:b300:8 CPUs= RealMemory= State=UNKNOWN PartitionName=gpu Nodes=gpu[01-04] Default=YES MaxTime=3-00:00:00 State=UP \ TRESBillingWeights="CPU=0.0625,Mem=0.0026G,GRES/gpu=1.0" # Accounting and enforcement of limits AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu,gres/gpu:b300 AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits,qos,safe # Priority PriorityType=priority/multifactor PriorityFlags=MAX_TRES PriorityDecayHalfLife=14-0 PriorityCalcPeriod=5 PriorityMaxAge=7-0 PriorityWeightFairshare=100000 PriorityWeightQOS=20000 PriorityWeightAge=5000 PriorityWeightJobSize=0 PriorityWeightPartition=0 # Preemption PreemptType=preempt/qos PreemptMode=REQUEUE PreemptExemptTime=00:30:00 JobRequeue=1 # Isolation ProctrackType=proctrack/cgroup TaskPlugin=task/cgroup,task/affinity Reading notes:
select/cons_tres is required for sharing GRES (MPS, shard) [5] and for the preemption of heterogeneous jobs [3]. AccountingStorageTRES: declare gres/gpu and its typed variant, as the documentation recommends [6]. Declaring gres/gpu also enables gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil [6]. AccountingStorageEnforce=...,safe: a job starts only if it can finish within its limits in TRES-minutes [4]. The fair-share weight dominates (100,000); the QOS weight (20,000) breaks ties; age (5,000) prevents starvation of an old job.
data.split#Splitting between batch and infere:
The inference service is a common good: its GPUs are taken from each share in proportion to ownership. With an inference pool of 16 GPUs (2 servers, 2 TP=8 instances):
Total share of which inference (pro rata) Guaranteed batch A 26 13 G_A = 13 B 6 3 G_B = 3 Service – – G_S = 16 With a pool of 8 GPUs the pro rata gives 6.5 and 1.5, so it is rounded to G_A = 19 and G_B = 5: fair-share, which counts continuously, rebalances the half GPU over time. The inference pool can change size with the time of day (elastic pool); the GPUs released go to borrow jobs.
data.the-qos#The QOS: QOS Cap Role instA GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_A A’s share, never preempted instB GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_B B’s share, never preempted service GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_S shared vLLM instances, never preempted borrow none surplus; preemptible by the three QOS above; ordered by fair-share GrpTRES limits the total TRES allocated to all running jobs of the QOS [4]. Since G_A + G_B + G_S = 32, the sum of the guaranteed shares never exceeds the cluster. The GPUs an owner does not occupy are either free or held by borrow jobs, therefore recoverable by preemption.
data.user-side#User side: # Within one's guaranteed share (default QOS) sbatch -A a_physics --gres=gpu:b300:4 train.sh # Beyond one's share: borrowing, preemptible, must be able to resume sbatch -A a_physics --qos=borrow --requeue --gres=gpu:b300:8 \ --signal=B:TERM@300 train_checkpoint.sh The script of a borrow job traps SIGTERM, writes a checkpoint within the 300 s of GraceTime, and restarts from the last checkpoint when requeued.
data.weekly-reservation#B’s big jobs: a weekl:
B’s guaranteed share (G_B = 3 or 5) is below 8. Without a special measure, B can run a job on a whole server (TP=8, multi-GPU training) only in the borrow QOS, hence with no guaranteed delay. B is given a recurring reservation of one whole server.
# A 48 h window every week, starting Monday 8:00, for institution B scontrol create reservation ReservationName=instB_weekly \ StartTime=2026-11-02T08:00:00 Duration=2-00:00:00 Flags=WEEKLY \ Accounts=instB PartitionName=gpu NodeCnt=1 # On B's side, during the window sbatch -A b_lab --reservation=instB_weekly --qos=borrow \ --gres=gpu:b300:8 --time=2-00:00:00 training.sh Slurm’s behaviour, from the reservation documentation [21]:
WEEKLY makes the reservation recurring: it activates and deactivates itself every week. During the window, the reserved resources serve only the reservation’s jobs: “no other jobs can use those resources”. Unused reserved time is charged to the reservation’s users or accounts, in equal parts. Here all of it goes to instB. B therefore pays for its window in fair-share whether it uses it or not. That is fair (the server was taken from the others) and it encourages reserving only what will be used. B submits in the borrow QOS, not in instB whose 3-GPU cap would block an 8-GPU job. The preemption risk is nil: no owner job of A can enter the reserved server. Sizing. B’s weekly share is 6 x 168 = 1,008 GPU-hours. A 48 h window costs 8 x 48 = 384 GPU-hours, 38 % of its share. The rest is consumed in instB and borrow. The agreement fixes the duration; a 126 h window would exhaust all of B’s share in a whole server.
Before each window, Slurm must start on the chosen server only jobs that finish before it opens. borrow jobs that declare a short --time then keep filling that server until the last minute. This behaviour is verified in the acceptance tests (test 9). For B, the job must also fit the window: --time less than or equal to the remaining duration.

data.continue#Code assistant: the Continue ex:
Continue accepts any OpenAI-compatible provider, LiteLLM and vLLM included: provider: openai with a custom apiBase [16]. The configuration file (~/.continue/config.yaml by default) requires the fields name, version and schema. Each model declares roles among chat, autocomplete, embed, rerank, edit, apply and summarize [17].
name: B300 platform version: 1.0.0 schema: v1 models: - name: Large model (B300) provider: openai model: large-model # model_name exposed by the gateway apiBase: https://llm.example.org/v1 apiKey: ${{ secrets.B300_GATEWAY_KEY }} roles: [chat, edit, apply, summarize] defaultCompletionOptions: contextLength: 131072 maxTokens: 4096 - name: Fast completion (B300) provider: openai model: small-code-model apiBase: https://llm.example.org/v1 apiKey: ${{ secrets.B300_GATEWAY_KEY }} roles: [autocomplete] The key is the user’s virtual key, attached to the team of their institution: their consumption lands in the right share. It is referenced as a secret (${{ secrets.... }} [17]), never written in clear in a versioned file. Autocompletion sends a request on every keystroke. Serve it with a small dedicated model (an instance of a few GPUs, or MIG) and set an rpm_limit on the key, or it will eat the institution’s quota. contextLength must not exceed the vLLM instance’s --max-model-len.
data.remote-ssh#Development and jobs: Remote-:
Remote-SSH reads the user’s ~/.ssh/config [18]. Target the login node, never a GPU node: GPU nodes are reached only through a Slurm job, otherwise the work escapes fair-share and cgroup isolation.
# ~/.ssh/config Host b300-bastion HostName bastion.example.org User alice IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_b300 Host b300-login HostName login.b300.internal User alice IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_b300 ProxyJump b300-bastion // settings.json (VS Code, user) { "remote.SSH.remotePlatform": { "b300-login": "linux" }, "remote.SSH.remoteServerListenOnSocket": true } remote.SSH.remotePlatform fixes the host type [18]. The login node is shared by many users: the documentation then recommends enabling Remote Server Listen On Socket for security [18].
The VS Code server consumes CPU and memory on the login node. Set per-user limits on that node (systemd cgroups) so that one session does not penalise the others. Do not run computation on the login node: go through srun/sbatch.
data.vscode#Access from VS Code: Two uses, two paths: the code assistant talks to the gateway over HTTPS; development and job submission go over SSH to the login node.
